rows.reviewerNote: Read as the child meets it: BEARD fits 'a long white ___ on his chin'. BOARD makes no sense there under any reading, and BELOD is not a word, so there is exactly one defensible answer. Checked: every value put in the gap; the key EAR is a familiar three-letter word making an everyday target; lexicon confirms the word and non-word status of all six strings. The sentence is 10 words with a full stop and no dash, in British English. The walk has three sentences of 10, 11 and 10 words; it rules out the non-word by the rule, then the real word by the sentence, names BEARD, and does not use 'wrong'. No surface pattern gives the key away: EAR and OAR share an ending, so that ending does not single out the key.

changes.before: Three letters that make a word are missing. Which three?
changes.after: Three letters are missing from the word in capitals. Together they spell a word. Which three?

changes.before: Mum spread butter on a thick slice of BR___ for my lunch.
changes.after: Grandad has a long white B___D on his chin.

changes.before: The gap comes after 'slice of'. Mum spreads butter for our lunch. “ead” fills it to make “bread” for eating. Those two form real words, yet none suits here.
changes.after: “elo” is not a word, so it cannot be the answer. “oar” makes “board”, but nobody has a board on their chin. “ear” makes “beard”, the hair that grows on a chin.

changes.before: Does not fit the sentence, although it makes a real word (BROWN).
changes.after: OAR is itself a word and makes BOARD, a real word, but a board is not something a person has on their chin. Tagged ignores-sentence: the child built a word without checking the sentence.

changes.before: Does not fit the sentence, although it makes a real word (BROKE).
changes.after: ELO is not a word, and in the gap it makes BELOD, which is not a word either. Tagged fits-gap-not-word: the child filled the gap without using the little-word rule.
